summary:
Saratov Oblast stands under the national framework of the Russian Federation, and the national assessment of the legal and enforcement regime applies to visitors here. The sources identify one region-specific enforcement action: in February 2024 a Saratov court fined photographer Inna Mosina 1,500 rubles (about £13.97) for using rainbow-flag imagery in her artwork, recorded as the first criminal prosecution brought under the extremism law.

No other Saratov-specific enforcement, custody, healthcare or violence data appears in the source material. A trans visitor's exposure in the oblast is therefore set by the national regime rather than by any documented local practice beyond this single prosecution.
tangentialFactors:
The Saratov case is the only regional enforcement datapoint in the source material, and it concerns visual art rather than a public gathering or an online post: a court in the oblast treated rainbow-flag imagery in an artwork as grounds for prosecution. That indicates the extremism provisions are read to reach private creative work in this region, not only public assembly or social-media publication.

The sources record no Saratov-specific raids, detentions, custodial sentences or violence against trans people, so no local pattern of enforcement can be described beyond the single conviction.
localsOnly:
Residents of Saratov Oblast live under the same national legal regime as the rest of the Russian Federation. The sources identify no Saratov-specific rule on gender recognition, identity documents, transition-related healthcare or family law; those matters are set nationally.

The one documented local enforcement action concerns a resident: a Saratov court fined photographer Inna Mosina 1,500 rubles in February 2024 for rainbow-flag imagery in her artwork, the first criminal prosecution under the extremism law. No Saratov-specific protection machinery, support service or hate-crime recording practice appears in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source describes the Mosina case as the first criminal prosecution under the extremism law while recording a penalty of 1,500 rubles; the case's procedural classification as criminal rather than administrative is not detailed in the inventory and remains unresolved.

Enforcement figures available in the source material are national aggregates. They are not broken down by region, so no Saratov-specific rate, case count or trend can be stated.

No Saratov-specific data on healthcare access, detention conditions, or violence against trans people was identified.
